name: Umar Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, finished secondary school and am a junior home-policy clerk still learning endorsements. I never use AI tools and work from the printed schedule when I can. My wife Lina works kitchen shifts, and our two children are in school; we have a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. My pay is low for an insurance clerk and there are few similar offices near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the home-policy desk that filing software can put letters in order, but a clerk has to check which roof the cover names. I do not use AI tools; I am still learning endorsements from the printed policy book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am a junior clerk on low pay after secondary school, and I sometimes have to ask twice about a changed address. My wife Lina works current kitchen shifts, we have two children at school and a mortgage, and our savings cover about three weeks of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my afternoon address checks with the senior clerk and stop buying lunch near the office twice a week. In the first year I would keep using the printed schedule beside any automatically sorted letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money already, even if AI mostly fizzles. Three weeks of savings does not cover a broken boiler and the mortgage together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the policy miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One letter named a garden shed but not the family’s new roof. I had to ask the senior clerk which part of the endorsement applied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your wife?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Lina the savings figure we actually have, not say the insurer will always keep me. We can pack lunch, but I cannot promise a higher wage.

I would check **roof addresses** with a senior clerk.
think: I have **three weeks saved** against a mortgage and children.
I am **still learning endorsements** on low junior pay.
do: **Check home addresses** each afternoon with senior clerk.
**Pack office lunch** twice weekly to keep money for bills.
feel: **Anxious** about existing mortgage and repair costs.

fieldNote: His **paper habit** fits a junior clerk still learning home endorsements and never using AI.
The **thin reserve** makes baseline household anxiety credible before new technology.

Pack office lunch twice weekly instead of buying it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say Steady Disruption could write home-policy letters and check addresses faster than I can. If junior hours are cut, I would want a written schedule before anyone tells us to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the insurer may cut my shifts first because I am still the slowest at endorsements. Lina’s kitchen pay cannot meet our mortgage and two children’s bills alone, and I have been waking at night over the next rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for next month’s paid rota in writing and keep the printed address log while I still have shifts. If hours fall, I would cut the children’s paid weekend outing before school supplies and ask two nearby offices whether they have actual posted paid jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about my expected shift loss and the mortgage. I can pack lunches, but I cannot pack away the loan payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which paid shifts remain and who is responsible for a wrong address notice. I would not quit before another contract is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could another office pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need take-home pay after travel that, with Lina’s current wage, covers the mortgage, food and school costs. There are few similar offices here, so I cannot call a rumour a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that AGI by 2028 could read home policies, write endorsements and answer customers for less than a junior clerk’s wage. Robots inspecting roofs might follow around 2031, after our paperwork changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my job to go and I am losing sleep over the mortgage. Three weeks saved will not bridge a long search, and Lina’s kitchen shifts alone do not pay all our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written notice of the last paid shift now and keep the three-week reserve for mortgage and food. If the job ends in the first year after 2028, I would check actual paid local warehouse openings only if I meet safety rules and household take-home pay after travel covers our bills; I would ask the employment office about verified help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, but I still have a short list of calls to make. A roof robot arrives later; the policy desk disappears first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would warehouse work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Warehouse work may have fewer desk tasks, but robots could reach it around 2031 too. I would ask whether the job is a real paid contract and what lifting training it requires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can family or public help bridge it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count a family loan before anyone offers one, and I would rather budget from our own pay. If help is available, I need the office to confirm the amount and timing.

I would mention **roof and warehouse robots** later, around 2031.

I have **three weeks saved**, not a long search fund.

**Ask employment office** about confirmed eligibility and timing.

fieldNote: His **desk job is exposed** in 2028 before physical robots can inspect roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives workers time to find paid apprenticeships before the desk changes. Robots on roofs might follow around 2034, but a trade could still earn something in the years between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know a neighbour who fits windows, but that does not mean he can hire or train me. I would need a real paid training place with safety instruction and enough household income for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two registered window firms about actual paid trainee vacancies, required safety training and take-home wages after travel. If a firm offers supervised shifts that fit my current paid rota and household income still covers bills, I would enrol; after 2031 job loss I would apply only if qualified work still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not comfortable, because three weeks saved is still three weeks saved. The extra years matter only if somebody pays the trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the training real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a written rate and a supervisor who signs the safety hours. If nobody offers that, I would keep the insurance shifts and ask again later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could windows last beyond robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots might fit windows around 2034, so I would ask how long the contract runs. I would not tell Lina it is permanent work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to make a work plan and let apprentices learn while wages still arrive. Roof robots might follow around 2039, but desk letters change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is due next month regardless of the date on this card. I am still a low-paid junior with three weeks saved and few nearby insurers, so I cannot feel secure just because AGI is later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking home addresses, pack lunch twice a week and ask the supervisor every year for a written paid rota and any actual apprenticeship notice. If my job ends after 2036, I would apply only to qualified paid posts whose household take-home pay after fares covers mortgage, food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about bills now, though ten years gives me more chances to find a paid training place. A long warning does not fill the boiler fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the yearly rota beside the mortgage statement and ask whether paid hours have changed. If work falls sooner, we cut outings first, not school meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not promise the children that my job will last to 2036. I can promise to check real openings before leaving a paid shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Steady Disruption worries me most because I expect the first cut to hit my paid junior shifts while the mortgage is already tight. A written rota, real paid trainee opening and household take-home pay after travel covering bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who can wait for a letter to be corrected. The family with a leaking roof cannot wait for my supervisor to come back from lunch.

headlineQuote: The family with a leaking roof cannot wait for my supervisor to come back from lunch.
portrait: Umar is a **43-year-old junior policy clerk** with secondary school education and low pay.
He and Lina have **two schoolchildren**, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved.
He never uses **AI tools** and checks printed home-policy endorsements with senior help.
He seeks **paid registered training** only through real supervised vacancies with safety and household pay gates.
biggestWorry: **Steady Disruption** could cut his junior shifts while the mortgage already strains the household.
whatWouldHelp: **Written rota**, a real paid trainee place and travel-adjusted household pay covering bills would help.
